docs.title: 📌 Executive Summary & Architectural Philosophy
docs.text:
Modern on-demand food delivery and dispatch platforms commonly fail when deployed into sovereign, air-gapped, or resource-constrained local development environments. These failures stem from three acute distributed systems anti-patterns:

  1. Latitude Area Distortion in Geospatial Engines: Most commercial tutorials store delivery boundaries in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857). Because Web Mercator projects the Earth onto a flat cylinder, scale distortion accelerates with latitude (\(k = \sec\phi\)). At \(37.77^\circ\text{N}\) (San Francisco), areas are distorted by \(+59.6\%\); at \(51.5^\circ\text{N}\) (London), distortion exceeds \(+158\%\), falsely rejecting valid customer addresses or including unreachable ocean locations.
  2. Thundering Herd Dispatch Contention: Broadcasting orders to all couriers simultaneously causes severe lock contention, cellular connection churn, and driver rejection fatigue.
  3. Transactional Outbox WAL Bloat: High-throughput transactional outbox tables that clean up old events using standard SQL DELETE queries trigger massive PostgreSQL MVCC dead-tuple churn, bloat Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), and invalidate downstream Change Data Capture (CDC) replication slots.

This platform resolves these challenges by strictly enforcing six non-negotiable architectural contracts:

│                                NON-NEGOTIABLE CONTRACTS                                │
├────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┤
│  1. 100% Sovereign         │  2. Single Host Ingress    │  3. Geodesic CRS Precision   │
│  Zero public cloud SaaS    │  Port 8080 host-bound only │  EPSG:4326 PostGIS only      │
│  Local boundary mocks      │  CNI encapsulated routing  │  ST_Covers on WGS 84 Spheroid│
├────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│  4. Targeted 1-to-1 Lease  │  5. Zero-WAL Outbox Prune  │  6. Hardware Acceleration    │

docs.title: 1. Geodesic CRS Precision (geography(Polygon, 4326) vs geometry(3857))
docs.text:
• Storing service zones in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) introduces up to \(+60\%\) scale distortion at non-equatorial latitudes.
  • All service zones and customer coordinates are strictly typed as geography(Polygon, 4326) and geography(Point, 4326).
  • Containment queries execute natively on the WGS 84 ellipsoid via ST_Covers: 
    SELECT r.id, r.name FROM restaurants r
WHERE r.is_active = true
  AND ST_Covers(r.delivery_zone, ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(-122.4194, 37.7749), 4326)::geography);
  • Unlike ST_Contains (which excludes perimeter edges), ST_Covers satisfies boundary closure: points lying directly on the delivery border evaluate to TRUE.

docs.title: 2. Two-Stage Spatial Resolution (Uber H3 Res 8 + PostGIS Fine)
docs.text:
• Stage 1 (Coarse In-Memory Filter): Customer coordinates map to a 64-bit integer H3 cell in \(O(1)\) CPU time. A 1-ring expansion (kRing(H3, 1)) retrieves candidate restaurants within 7 discrete hexagons.
  • Stage 2 (Fine Geodesic Containment): Only the filtered candidate restaurants are evaluated with PostGIS ST_Covers, reducing spatial query latency from \(O(N)\) polygon intersections to \(O(1)\) indexed integer lookups.

docs.title: 3. Zero-WAL Transactional Outbox Partition Pruning
docs.text:
• High-volume order processing writes outbox events within the same ACID transaction as the order.
  • Conventional systems run DELETE FROM outbox_events WHERE created_at < ..., causing massive PostgreSQL dead-tuple bloat (n_dead_tup), autovacuum page-locking, and WAL stream saturation.
  • This platform declaratively partitions outbox_events by daily range: 
    CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    id UUID NOT NULL,
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
  • A scheduled daemon drops partitions older than 7 days via DROP TABLE <partition_name>;. This triggers an OS filesystem unlink() on the physical storage file, generating n_dead_tup == 0 and zero WAL amplification.

docs.title: 1. Architectural Philosophy & Non-Negotiable Contracts
docs.text:
Modern on-demand food delivery and dispatch platforms commonly fail when deployed into sovereign, air-gapped, or resource-constrained local environments. These failures trace back to three fatal distributed systems anti-patterns:

  1. Spatial Boundary Distortion via Planar Projections: Naive geospatial implementations store geographic boundaries using Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) for simple Euclidean planar calculations. Because Web Mercator projects the Earth onto a flat cylinder, scale distortion accelerates with latitude (\(k = \sec(\phi)\)). In cities like London (\(51.5^\circ\text{N}\)) or Seattle (\(47.6^\circ\text{N}\)), planar distance and area calculations produce \(+48\%\) to \(+60\%\) distortion, causing delivery perimeters to falsely reject valid customer dropoffs or include unserviceable locations.
  2. Thundering Herd Dispatch Contention & Driver Fatigue: Broadcasting order offers to all active couriers within a radius creates extreme database lock contention, packet storms on mobile cellular connections, and driver fatigue caused by millisecond race conditions where acceptance clicks fail.
  3. Database Write Amplification via Transactional Outbox Bloat: Implementing the Transactional Outbox pattern with SQL DELETE queries on high-throughput event tables triggers severe PostgreSQL Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) dead-tuple churn. Dead tuples bloat disk pages, exhaust the autovacuum daemon, saturate the Write-Ahead Log (WAL), and invalidate downstream Change Data Capture (CDC) replication slots.

To eliminate these failure modes, this platform enforces six non-negotiable architectural contracts:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                NON-NEGOTIABLE CONTRACTS                                │
├────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┤

│  Zero public cloud SaaS    │  Port 8080 host-bound only │  EPSG:4326 PostGIS only      │

docs.title: ADR-001: Geodesic Ellipsoidal Calculations (geography(4326)) vs Web Mercator (geometry(3857))
docs.text:
• Context: A food delivery system must calculate whether a customer's delivery location falls within a restaurant's service boundary polygon. Geospatial software often stores coordinates in planar Cartesian coordinates (EPSG:3857) for computational convenience.
  • Problem: Earth is an oblate spheroid, not a cylinder. The scale factor \(k\) of Web Mercator grows as a function of latitude \(\phi\): $\(k = \sec(\phi) = \frac{1}{\cos(\phi)}\)$ At latitude \(37.7749^\circ\text{N}\) (San Francisco), differential scale distortion is: $\(\Delta_{\text{scale}} = \frac{1}{\cos(37.7749^\circ)} - 1 \approx 1.263 - 1 = +26.3\%\)$ Area calculations distort quadratically: $\(\Delta_{\text{area}} = k^2 - 1 = (1.263)^2 - 1 \approx +59.5\%\)$ Storing boundaries in EPSG:3857 causes severe false positives and false negatives on delivery perimeters.
  • Decision: All restaurant delivery boundaries and customer dropoff locations are strictly typed as geography(Polygon, 4326) and geography(Point, 4326).
  • Mathematical Invariant: Spatial containment is evaluated using PostGIS native ST_Covers(geog1, geog2) directly on the WGS 84 ellipsoid (\(a = 6,378,137.0\text{ m}\), \(f = 1/298.257223563\)). Unlike ST_Contains (which excludes points lying directly on the perimeter boundary \(\partial P\)), ST_Covers satisfies the closed topological property: $\(\forall p \in \partial P \implies \text{ST\_Covers}(P, p) = \text{TRUE}\)$
  • Consequence: Sub-millimeter spatial accuracy with zero projection coordinate distortion at query time.

docs.title: ADR-002: Two-Stage Spatial Resolution (Uber H3 Res 8 Coarse + PostGIS Geodesic Fine)
docs.text:
• Context: Evaluating PostGIS geodesic point-in-polygon calculations across thousands of restaurant delivery zones on every catalog request or video feed scroll induces high CPU utilization on PostgreSQL.
  • Decision: We implement a Two-Stage Spatial Indexing Pipeline:
  • Stage 1: Coarse Discrete Global Grid (Uber H3 Resolution 8):
    • Hexagonal global tessellation where customer coordinates and restaurant centroids map to 64-bit integer H3 indices in \(O(1)\) memory time.
    • At Resolution 8, average hexagon area is \(0.737\text{ km}^2\) with an edge length of \(\approx 461.4\text{ meters}\).
    • Fast spatial candidate lookup computes a 1-ring neighborhood: $\(\text{Candidates} = \text{kRing}(H3_{\text{customer}}, k=1) \implies 7 \text{ discrete cells}\)$
  • Stage 2: Geodesic Ellipsoidal Containment (PostGIS ST_Covers):
    • Candidate restaurants identified in Stage 1 undergo exact geodesic verification against the geography(Polygon, 4326) boundary: 
      SELECT id, name FROM restaurants
WHERE h3_res8 = :customer_h3
  AND is_active = true
  AND ST_Covers(delivery_zone, :customer_dropoff_geog);
  • Consequence: Spatial candidate retrieval drops from \(O(N)\) polygon boundary scans to \(O(1)\) B-Tree integer lookups followed by targeted geodesic checks on \(\le 5\) candidate rows.

docs.title: ADR-003: Deterministic 1-to-1 Dispatch Lease State Machine vs Thundering Herd Broadcast
docs.text:
• Context: Delivery platforms that broadcast incoming orders to all couriers in a radius suffer from:
  • Thundering Herd Concurrency: Dozens of drivers attempt to claim the same order concurrently, creating row-level database lock contention.
  • Driver Frustration: Couriers who click "Accept" 50ms late receive "Order already claimed" errors.
  • Cellular Battery Drain: High-frequency WebSocket broadcasts keep mobile cellular radios in continuous high-power transmission mode.
  • Decision: We implement an exclusive, targeted 1-to-1 Dispatch Lease State Machine:
  • The dispatch engine ranks nearby couriers using H3 spatial binning and Valhalla road-network travel times.
  • The top candidate receives an exclusive 30-second server-authoritative lease.
  • During this 30-second window, no other courier can view or accept the order.
  • Database claim atomicity is enforced via an optimistic conditional update: 
    UPDATE orders
SET courier_id = :courierId,
    status = 'DISPATCHED',
    version = version + 1,
    updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = :orderId
  AND courier_id IS NULL
  AND dispatch_lease_expires_at > NOW();
  • If the 30-second lease expires without courier acceptance, a background scheduler revokes the lease and tenders the offer to candidate \(N+1\).
  • Consequence: Zero race conditions, zero dual-assignments, and deterministic state progression.

docs.title: ADR-004: Zero-WAL Transactional Outbox Pruning via Daily Range DROP TABLE
docs.text:
• Context: In microservice architectures, updating business tables and publishing events to Apache Kafka must be atomic (Transactional Outbox pattern). Events are written to an outbox_events table within the same ACID transaction as the business entity.
  • The PostgreSQL Dead-Tuple WAL Problem:
  • High-volume order processing writes 25,000+ outbox events daily.
  • Standard retention jobs run DELETE FROM outbox_events WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'.
  • In PostgreSQL MVCC, DELETE does not free disk space; it marks tuples as dead, writes deletion records to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL), bloats table pages, and delays replication slot advances.
  • Under heavy local load testing, autovacuum cannot keep up, causing replication slot bloat and disk saturation.
  • Decision: We implement Zero-WAL Outbox Partition Pruning:
  • The outbox_events table is declaratively partitioned by daily range: 
    CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    id UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
  • Physical partitions are named deterministically: outbox_events_yYYYYmMMdDD (e.g. outbox_events_y2026m10d21).
  • Upcoming partitions are automatically created 14 days in advance by a scheduled Spring task.
  • A scheduled Spring daemon identifies partitions older than 7 days and executes DROP TABLE <partition_name>;.
  • Verification Proof: DROP TABLE issues an OS filesystem unlink on the partition's physical storage file (relfilenode). It eliminates page scanning, generates zero dead tuples (n_dead_tup == 0), and avoids WAL write amplification.

docs.title: ADR-005: Single Host Port Ingress (8080) & Kubernetes CNI Encapsulation
docs.text:
• Context: The platform contains 15+ microservices, datastores, consoles, and streaming brokers. In local workstation development (k3s, Kind, Minikube), binding individual container ports to the host machine causes port collisions with developer tools, SSH daemons, or system web servers.
  • Decision: Exactly one single port (8080) is bound to the host workstation.
  • A Kubernetes Ingress Controller (Ingress-Nginx) manages the host gateway.
  • All internal services communicate strictly over the internal Kubernetes Container Network Interface (CNI) pod network via ClusterIP Services and CoreDNS (<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local).
  • Path-based routing, CORS enforcement, and WebSocket protocol upgrading occur at this gateway.
  • Consequence: Complete workstation isolation, zero port collisions, and identical networking semantics between local testing and production Kubernetes clusters.

docs.title: ADR-006: Hardware GPU Passthrough with Internal Concurrency Scaling (AMD RX 7900 GRE)
docs.text:
• Context: Short-form video reels uploaded by restaurant merchants must be transcoded into multi-bitrate HLS streams (1080p, 720p, 480p). Transcoding on CPU cores exhausts workstation CPU budgets. The host workstation contains an AMD Radeon RX 7900 GRE (RDNA 3 / Navi 31 XL) with Dual VCN 4.0 hardware video engines.
  • Constraint: Kubernetes Device Plugins allocate GPU devices as indivisible whole units (amd.com/gpu: 1). Setting replicas: 2 causes the second pod to hang in Pending state.
  • Decision:
  • The worker Deployment runs with replicas: 1.
  • Mounts /dev/dri/card0 and /dev/dri/renderD128 with GIDs for video (44) and render (107).
  • Internal concurrency is scaled via RabbitMQ prefetch_count: 4.
  • Up to 4 hardware VAAPI FFmpeg encoding pipelines run simultaneously across the Dual VCN 4.0 engines. Excess encoding jobs queue safely in RabbitMQ without dropping frames or overloading silicon.

docs.title: B. ISO 19107 Geographic Information Domain Conceptual Model
docs.text: The domain model follows ISO 19107 geometric schema primitives: - GeoPoint (DirectPosition): Coordinates defined as latitude (\(\phi\)) and longitude (\(\lambda\)) on the WGS 84 Reference Ellipsoid. - DeliveryBoundary (GM_Polygon): Surface boundary bounded by an exterior linear ring \(\partial P\). - Boundary Containment Rule (Invariant BR-GEO-01): An order \(O\) for restaurant \(R\) with dropoff point \(p\) is legally dispatchable if and only if \(p\) lies within or on the closure of \(R\)'s delivery zone: $\(p \in \overline{\text{zone}(R)} \iff \text{ST\_Covers}(\text{zone}(R), p) = \text{TRUE}\)$

docs.title: C. Ubiquitous Domain Vocabulary & Semantic Invariants
docs.text: Domain Concept Definition & Semantic Role Formal Invariant Contract Restaurant Boundary Closed geodesic polygon on WGS 84 within which the merchant guarantees food freshness. BR-GEO-01: Boundary must be simple, planar-valid, and oriented counter-clockwise without self-intersections. Dropoff Coordinates Latitude, longitude, plus human vertical access indicators (building name, floor, room number, gate code). BR-ORD-01: Dropoff point must be covered by the restaurant's active delivery boundary at checkout time. Dispatch Lease A 30-second exclusive reservation issued to exactly one courier candidate at a time. BR-DSP-01: \(\forall \text{Order } O, \sum \text{ActiveLeases}(O) \le 1\). No concurrent offers permitted. Verification PIN A cryptographically secure 6-digit random code generated at checkout and known only to the customer. BR-SEC-01: PIN handshake required at doorstep. Courier cannot mark DELIVERED without customer PIN. Escrow Account An internal double-entry ledger account holding customer funds during order fulfillment. BR-FIN-01: \(\sum \text{Debits} - \sum \text{Credits} = 0\). Zero negative balances permitted.

docs.title: Why DROP TABLE instead of DELETE?
docs.text:
Standard SQL DELETE FROM outbox_events WHERE created_at < ... queries generate massive amounts of MVCC dead-tuple churn, forcing the PostgreSQL autovacuum daemon into aggressive cycles and generating redundant WAL records.

In this architecture, outbox_events is partitioned daily: 

CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    id UUID NOT NULL,
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

When partitions exceed the 7-day retention window, the Spring scheduler issues:

This reclaims disk blocks instantly on the underlying filesystem with zero dead rows (n_dead_tup == 0) and minimal WAL write volume.

docs.text: Sovereign Hyper-Local Video & Food Delivery Platform Deep Systems Engineering Handbook: Geospatial Differential Geometry, Discrete Global Grids, Storage Engine Mechanics & Concurrency Theory

docs.title: 1. Deep-Dive 1: Geodesic Differential Geometry vs Web Mercator Distortion
1.1 The Mathematical Fallacy of Planar Projections in Hyper-Local Delivery
docs.text:
Commercial geospatial applications frequently make the catastrophic mistake of projecting spherical Earth coordinates \((\phi, \lambda)\) into Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) to perform planar Euclidean geometry.

The forward projection from geodetic latitude \(\phi\) and longitude \(\lambda\) to Web Mercator Cartesian coordinates \((x, y)\) is defined as:

\[x = R \cdot \lambda$$ $$y = R \cdot \ln\left[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\phi}{2}\right)\right]\]

where \(R = 6,378,137.0\text{ meters}\) is the semi-major equatorial radius.

The differential scale factor \(k\) is given by the derivative of arc length:

\[k(\phi) = \sec(\phi) = \frac{1}{\cos(\phi)}\]

Because distance distorts by \(k\), area distorts quadratically by \(k^2\):

\[\text{Area Factor}(\phi) = \frac{1}{\cos^2(\phi)}\]

docs.title: 1.3 The Production Consequence
docs.text:
If a restaurant in San Francisco sets a delivery boundary as a \(2.0\text{ km}\) circle in EPSG:3857, the actual physical ground radius covered is only \(1.58\text{ km}\)—a loss of nearly \(420\text{ meters}\) in every direction!

Customers standing \(1.7\text{ km}\) away from the restaurant are falsely told: "You are outside the delivery area." Conversely, if the zone is scaled up to compensate, drivers are assigned to addresses located in the Pacific Ocean or across uncrossable water bodies.

docs.title: 1.4 PostGIS Ellipsoidal Geodesic Realization (geography(4326))
docs.text:
To eliminate projection distortion, this platform mandates that all spatial columns use geography(Polygon, 4326) and geography(Point, 4326).

PostGIS computes distance and containment directly on the WGS 84 Spheroid using Vincenty's inverse formula and Karney's geodesic algorithms: - Semi-major axis \(a = 6,378,137.0\text{ m}\) - Flattening \(f = \frac{1}{298.257223563}\) - Semi-minor axis \(b = a(1 - f) \approx 6,356,752.3142\text{ m}\)

Under this model, ST_Covers(delivery_zone, dropoff_location) evaluates whether the geodetic point lies strictly on the ellipsoidal surface enclosed by the geodesic polygon boundary, achieving sub-millimeter precision worldwide.

docs.title: 2. Deep-Dive 2: Uber H3 Discrete Global Grid Bitfield Mechanics
2.1 The Need for Coarse Hierarchical Binning
docs.text:
Executing exact PostGIS geodesic containment checks (ST_Covers) across \(10,000\) active restaurants requires \(O(N)\) computational complexity per user swipe. At 1,000 concurrent video reel viewers, this generates \(10^7\) geodesic intersection evaluations per second, saturating CPU caches.

We decouple spatial indexing into a Two-Stage Candidate Pipeline utilizing the Uber H3 Discrete Global Grid System.

docs.title: 2.2 64-Bit H3 Index Bitfield Layout
docs.text:
Every H3 cell is represented as a single unsigned 64-bit integer (uint64), bit-packed for instant in-memory comparison:

 0               1               2               3
 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
| Reserved | Mode | Edge |  Res  |   Base Cell   | Cell Digit 1 |
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
| Cell Digit 2  | Cell Digit 3  | ...           | Cell Digit 15 |
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
Field Name Bit Width Description Reserved 1 bit Reserved for future schema flags. Mode 4 bits Index mode (1 = Hexagon Cell, 2 = Directed Edge, 3 = Bidirectional Edge). Edge Mode 3 bits Sub-edge identifier (0 for cells). Resolution 4 bits Grid resolution level (\(0 \le \text{Res} \le 15\)). Stored as binary integer. Base Cell 7 bits One of 122 fundamental icosahedron base cells (\(0 \le \text{BaseCell} \le 121\)). Cell Digits 45 bits 15 resolution levels, each encoded as a 3-bit octal digit (\(0 \le d_i \le 6\)).

docs.title: 2.3 Selection of Resolution 8 for Hyper-Local Food & Video
docs.text:
In the H3 aperture 7 hierarchy, each finer resolution decomposes a hexagon into approximately 7 child hexagons:

\[A_{\text{child}} \approx \frac{1}{7} A_{\text{parent}}\]

At Resolution 8: - Average hexagon area: \(0.7373\text{ km}^2\) (\(737,327\text{ m}^2\)) - Hexagon edge length: \(\approx 461.4\text{ meters}\) - Hexagon diameter (vertex to vertex): \(\approx 922.8\text{ meters}\)

Resolution 8 aligns with the typical human walking and local delivery radius. When a customer opens the video feed: 1. The customer's coordinate is mapped to \(H3_{\text{cust}}\) in \(O(1)\) CPU time. 2. The candidate cell set is retrieved using a 1-ring expansion (kRing(H3, 1)), yielding exactly 7 discrete integers: $\(\text{Cells} = \{ H3_0, H3_1, H3_2, H3_3, H3_4, H3_5, H3_6 \}\)$ 3. The database executes an indexed integer equality join: 

SELECT id, name FROM restaurants 
WHERE h3_res8 IN (:h3_0, :h3_1, :h3_2, :h3_3, :h3_4, :h3_5, :h3_6)
  AND is_active = true
  AND ST_Covers(delivery_zone, :customer_dropoff);
4. The candidate pool is reduced from \(10,000\) to \(\approx 5\) candidate rows, resulting in \(99.95\%\) query pruning before geodesic evaluation occurs.

docs.title: 3. Deep-Dive 3: PostgreSQL MVCC, Write-Ahead Log (WAL) & Zero-WAL Partition Unlinking
3.1 PostgreSQL MVCC Heap Page Internals
docs.text:
PostgreSQL uses Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) to ensure readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Understanding why standard SQL DELETE queries destroy outbox performance requires inspecting the physical layout of a PostgreSQL 8KB Heap Page:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| PageHeaderData (24 bytes)                                         |
|  - pd_lsn (Log Sequence Number of last change)                    |
|  - pd_checksum, pd_flags, pd_lower, pd_upper, pd_special          |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ItemPointerData (Line Pointers: lp_offset, lp_flags, lp_len)      |
|  [Pointer 1] [Pointer 2] [Pointer 3] ... -----> (grows downward)  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     FREE SPACE REGION                             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| <----- (grows upward)                                             |
| Tuple Header (23 bytes): t_xmin, t_xmax, t_cid, t_infomask        |
| Tuple User Data (JSONB payload, UUIDs, Timestamps)                |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 3.2 The Disaster of Standard SQL DELETE on Outbox Tables
docs.text:
When a conventional background job cleans up processed outbox events via:

DELETE FROM outbox_events WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days';

PostgreSQL does not free disk space. Instead, it executes the following operations: 1. Locates every matching tuple and writes the current Transaction ID into t_xmax. 2. Marks the line pointer status as dead (LP_DEAD). 3. For every deleted row, generates a WAL deletion record and writes it to the WAL buffer. Under a load of 50,000 daily orders, this generates gigabytes of redundant WAL stream records. 4. Downstream Logical Replication Slots (pg_replication_slots) must process every single WAL deletion record, stalling Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines. 5. The heap page now contains dead tuples. The page cannot be truncated until the Autovacuum Daemon performs a full sequential page scan, updates the Free Space Map (FSM), and freezes transaction IDs.

docs.title: 3.3 The Zero-WAL Solution: Declarative Range Partition Unlinking
docs.text:
This platform eliminates MVCC dead-tuple churn entirely by declaratively partitioning outbox_events by daily range:

CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    id UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id UUID NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

Every physical partition is an autonomous relation on disk: - outbox_events_y2026m10d21 \(\rightarrow\) physical file base/16384/28491

When a daily partition exceeds the 7-day retention horizon:

DROP TABLE outbox_events_y2026m10d14;

The Physical OS Mechanics of DROP TABLE: 1. PostgreSQL removes the table entry from system catalogs (pg_class, pg_partitioned_table) in \(O(1)\) memory time. 2. PostgreSQL requests the Linux kernel to issue an unlink() system call on the physical file descriptor (relfilenode). 3. The ext4/XFS filesystem reclaims the underlying inode and data blocks immediately. 4. Metrics Result: - Dead tuples generated: n_dead_tup == 0 - Heap page scan cost: 0 pages read - WAL records generated: Negligible catalog metadata change - Replication slot lag: \(0\text{ ms}\)

docs.title: 4. Deep-Dive 4: Deterministic 1-to-1 Dispatch State Machine & Poisson Collision Probability
4.1 The Thundering Herd Failure Model
docs.text:
In naive food delivery systems, when an order reaches READY_FOR_PICKUP, the backend broadcasts an offer to all \(M\) active couriers within radius \(R\).

Assume driver acceptance attempts follow a Poisson arrival process with arrival rate \(\lambda = \frac{k}{\tau}\) (where \(k\) drivers attempt acceptance within network latency window \(\tau \approx 200\text{ ms}\)):

\[P(N \ge 2 \text{ claims in window } \tau) = 1 - e^{-\lambda \tau} - (\lambda \tau) e^{-\lambda \tau}\]

For a busy metropolitan sector where \(\lambda \tau = 3.5\):

\[P(\text{Collision}) = 1 - e^{-3.5} - 3.5 e^{-3.5} = 1 - 0.0302 - 0.1057 \approx 86.4\%\]

Under broadcast dispatch, \(86.4\%\) of orders experience high-concurrency race conditions. Drivers encounter screen freezes, database row locks stall HTTP threads, and \(M-1\) drivers experience psychological rejection fatigue.

docs.title: 4.2 The 1-to-1 Targeted Lease Protocol
docs.text:
We eliminate race conditions by transforming the dispatch problem from an uncoordinated competition into a deterministic, serialized token lease:

  1. Ranking Pipeline: $\(\text{Candidate Score} = w_1 \cdot \text{ETA}_{\text{Valhalla}} + w_2 \cdot \text{Rating} - w_3 \cdot \text{ActiveOrders}\)$
  2. Exclusive Lease Token: The top candidate (\(C_1\)) receives an exclusive lease token valid for exactly \(\Delta t = 30\text{ seconds}\): $\(\text{LeaseExpiry} = t_{\text{now}} + 30.0\text{s}\)$
  3. Database Guard Predicate: When courier \(C_1\) accepts the offer, the application executes an atomic conditional update: 
    UPDATE orders
SET courier_id = :courierId,
    status = 'DISPATCHED',
    version = version + 1,
    updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = :orderId
  AND courier_id IS NULL
  AND dispatch_lease_expires_at > NOW();
  4. Collision Probability: Because only candidate \(C_1\) holds the active lease token, the arrival rate for competing claims \(\lambda_{\text{competitors}} = 0\): $\(P(\text{Collision}) = 0.000000\%\)$
  5. Fault Recovery: If courier \(C_1\) does not accept within \(30.0\text{ seconds}\), the lease expires passively without requiring distributed distributed locks. The background DispatchLeaseEvictionDaemon detects that \(\text{LeaseExpiry} < t_{\text{now}}\) and advances the offer token to candidate \(C_2\).

5.1 Financial Integrity & The Elimination of Floating-Point Math
docs.text:
In distributed commerce, floating-point IEEE 754 arithmetic (float, double) is strictly banned due to binary representation errors:

// BANNED: IEEE 754 Floating-Point Error

System.out.println(a + b); // Prints: 0.30000000000000004

docs.title: 5.2 Immutable Double-Entry Ledger Mathematical Axiom
docs.text:
Every monetary transaction consists of balanced journal entries satisfying the fundamental accounting conservation equation:

\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Debits}_i - \sum_{j=1}^{m} \text{Credits}_j = 0.00\]
